a delivery robot doesn't live on a highway. it has to handle sidewalks, curb ramps, alleys and loading bays. satellites only see roofs, and mapping cars only see roads they can drive

that's the gap @vangrid_io is going after

instead of sending out fleets, it uses the phones people already carry. you walk slowly around a place, record a short clip and it gets rebuilt into a 3d model that robotics and ai teams pay for

» open https://t.co/xwNl3lg0dx in a browser or get the android app, ios is next

» pick a bounty on https://t.co/SlKeyio4aS record it and submit before the deadline
» if the requester accepts yours, you get paid in usdc on base

now here's what i'd be watching

their explorer shows 1.5m+ captures, about 490k wallets and over $740k in usdc put into bounties. every capture fingerprint is anchored on base, so you can check it yourself

they raised $9M from hashkey, animoca brands, https://t.co/zu5apI2jR6 capital, gate labs, borderless and mapleblock, and they're part of nvidia inception. ai agents can even hire a person to film a place now, paying in usdc on base or arc

of course, $VAN isn't live yet, their docs say points don't convert into $VAN and stronger anti-fake checks like device attestation haven't shipped

still, the biggest sensor network in the world might be the one already sitting in our pockets.

Nvidia should have died in 1997. A $1 million fake chip saved it.

The man who bought it resigned from Nvidia this week. His name is Jensen Huang.

In 1996, Nvidia was dying. Its first chip, the NV1, flopped. A second chip for Sega was abandoned. Jensen cut the company from about 100 people to around 40.

He had one more shot. It was called the RIVA 128.

Normally you design a chip, pay to build a physical prototype, test it, fix it, and build another. That takes months. He didn't have months.

So he bought a hardware emulator from a struggling company called IKOS for about $1 million. A fake chip built in code, the size of a refrigerator.

It was so slow the team sat waiting for a single frame of Windows to draw. They moved the ping-pong table so it would fit in the break room.

> They ran every game and driver they had on it
> They caught the bugs before any real chip existed
> Then Jensen skipped the prototype and went straight to mass production
> No one in the industry had done that before

If the first chips came back broken, Nvidia was finished.

They worked.

The RIVA 128 shipped in August 1997 with about one month of payroll left. It sold about a million units in four months. Nvidia went public in 1999.

For years, Jensen opened internal presentations with the same line: "Our company is thirty days from going out of business."

On November 12, 2026, Nvidia announced his resignation. He left a company worth about $4 trillion.

Most people wait for a perfect prototype before they ship anything. The company that powers AI exists because one founder couldn't afford to.

Would you have bet the company on the fake chip? Yes or no.

In 1996, Nvidia was about to go bankrupt.

Its lifeline was a deal with Sega, the video game giant behind Sonic. Nvidia was building the graphics chip for Sega's next game console.

For a tiny startup, it was everything. The deal was paying the bills.

A year in, Jensen Huang realized something terrible.

His team had built it wrong. Their whole approach to 3D graphics went against where the industry was heading.

Finishing the chip meant giving Sega a dead end. Stopping meant running out of money.

Either way, Nvidia was dead.

So Huang told Sega executive Shoichiro Irimajiri the truth. Nvidia couldn't finish the chip. Sega should find another partner.

Then he asked for something absurd.

Pay us anyway. Or we're out of business.

He even told Irimajiri the money would most likely be lost.

Irimajiri agreed. Sega invested $5 million in the company that had just failed it.

Huang said that money gave Nvidia "six months to live."

Nvidia used them to bet everything on a new chip, the RIVA 128. It came out in 1997 and shipped a million units in four months.

Nvidia was saved.

Sega later sold its shares for about $15 million.

Today, Nvidia is worth trillions.

Huang told this story at National Taiwan University's 2023 graduation. His lesson: confronting a mistake and asking for help saved the company.

Would you have told Sega the truth, or quietly finished the chip?

The API key is quietly on its way out. Brave put x402 on its Search API this week, so an agent pays per request in USDC with no account and no key. Short sentence, thirty year primitive inside it.

Keys exist because a server needed to know who you were in order to bill you. Identity was never the point. Billing was, and identity got bolted on because there was no way to collect money inside a request. Move payment to the request layer and the dependency falls apart. No signup, no dashboard, no monthly minimum, no human approving a developer account for a program that will exist for ninety seconds.

Then the other half, running the opposite direction. 6 in 10 onchain agent registrations now happen on @base through the ERC 8004 registry standard, and Rain shipped Agent Vaults so an agent can hold and spend under explicit controls. Identity is coming back, just unhooked from payment. You register not to be billed, but to be trusted.

Separating who you are from whether you can pay is the real unlock in this week's news, and almost nobody is framing it that way. Two different questions the web has spent thirty years answering with one login box.

Four stages cover the life of a tokenized asset. Injective's Veyra Upgrade fills in two of them.

Since June, @injective has shipped Vulcan and Meridian, launched Institutional Rail, and now voting on the Veyra mainnet upgrade is open.

If it passes, it will go live on November 24, 2026.

If you stake $INJ , you can vote on it. Here is what is on the ballot and why it matters 👇

✅ Where Veyra fits
Injective has been building toward one outcome: letting institutions handle a tokenized asset from start to finish on one chain. Meridian (IIP-701, live Sep 24, 2026, roughly 99% approval) added regulated token standards on the EVM and began testing private RFQ flows. Institutional Rail (Nov 2) gave banks and enterprises direct access to block production. Veyra builds on both.

✅ What Veyra adds

> IBC interoperability for Injective's EVM. Assets can move between the EVM and the wider IBC-connected ecosystem, so a tokenized asset issued on Injective can reach liquidity on other chains.

> RFQ infrastructure. A request for quote lets a trader ask for a firm price on a specific size and trade against it. Institutions use it for large orders, where working through a public order book can move the price.

> Expanded atomic swaps. Both sides of a swap settle together or not at all, so neither party carries the risk of delivering while the other does not.

> Privacy groundwork. Veyra builds on Meridian to prepare for CypherOS, Injective's planned native privacy platform. Institutions need to trade without exposing every position and counterparty on a public ledger.

✅ The pattern
Read the upgrades as a checklist for a tokenized asset's life:

- issue it (Meridian's regulated token standards), move it (IBC for the EVM),

- trade it (RFQ and atomic swaps), connect the institution (Institutional Rail),

- Protect the details (the privacy groundwork).

Each release fills in a stage, which prepares the chain for the institutional RWA launches Injective says are coming.

✅ What you can do
If you hold staked INJ, you can vote through the Injective Hub. Check the proposal there for the voting deadline. Staking directly keeps your governance vote, which INJC shares do not carry.
